sermon:
## The Prayer of an Empty Woman
*How God begins the deliverance of a nation in a place of unbearable weakness*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 1:1–2:11 · **Supporting:** Genesis 30:1–2; Luke 1:46–55; 1 Corinthians 1:27–29; Psalm 113:7–9

The book that gives Israel its first king does not open in a palace. It opens with a woman who cannot have a child, weeping at a doorpost while a priest mistakes her for a drunk.

**The empty are not the leftovers of the story. They are where it starts.**
The writer of 1 Samuel could have begun anywhere. He begins with Hannah. "He had two wives. The name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children" (1 Samuel 1:2). In a world that measured a woman's worth by the children at her feet, this is the writer telling us, before he tells us anything else, where God does His deepest work. Not in fullness. In emptiness.

And the emptiness is not abstract. It has a face, and the face is cruel. "Her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her, because the LORD had closed her womb" (1 Samuel 1:6). Year after year, at the one feast where the family was supposed to rejoice before God, Peninnah turned the knife. Hannah wept and would not eat. Even the husband who loved her could not reach the wound, "Am I not more to you than ten sons?" (1 Samuel 1:8). No. He was not. He was the comfort that does not comfort, because the ache was not for a husband. It was for a thing only God could open. This is not a new pattern. Rachel had stood here: "Give me children, or I shall die" (Genesis 30:1), and Jacob's anger burned, and he said, "Am I in the place of God?" The empty woman is one of Scripture's recurring doors, and behind every one of them God is about to do something the full could never receive.

**She does not curse God. She gives Him the wound.**
Watch what Hannah does with the pain, because it is the hinge of the whole chapter. She does not harden. She does not perform. She rises and goes to the house of the LORD and prays, and "she was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly" (1 Samuel 1:10). Her lips moved and no voice came, and Eli, the priest, the man whose job was to see, saw nothing. He thought she was drunk. The leadership of Israel could not tell the difference between a woman destroyed and a woman intoxicated. Remember that. We will meet Eli again, and his blindness will cost more than this.

And then the vow. "O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life" (1 Samuel 1:11). She asks for the one thing she cannot make happen, and in the same breath she gives it away. The son she has not yet conceived is already surrendered. This is not bargaining. Bargaining keeps the thing. Hannah opens her hands before they are ever filled. We pray to be filled so we can hold. She prayed to be filled so she could give. Those are not the same prayer.

And notice that God does not answer her in the moment. Eli, finally seeing past his own assumption, blesses her, "Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to him" (1 Samuel 1:17). Then comes the line that is easy to read past. "The woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad" (1 Samuel 1:18). Nothing had changed in her body yet. The womb was still closed. She had no child, no proof, no sign. What she had was a God she had handed the wound to, and that was enough to lift the grief off her face before the answer ever came. We wait for the circumstance to change before we will let the sorrow go. Hannah let it go at the altar. The peace came before the son did. It always does, for the one who has actually surrendered the thing.

**The God who hears the unheard is the God who comes for us in the manger.**
We build our churches for the Peninnahs, the fruitful, the visible, the ones with results to display. And I have done this. I have walked past the Hannahs in my own congregation, the ones moving their lips with no voice, and assumed, like Eli, that the silence meant nothing was happening. We mistake the loud for the alive. We measure by the womb that is full. God does not. "He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap" (Psalm 113:7).

And when the son comes, Samuel, "because I have asked for him from the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:20), Hannah sings, and her song is the seed of another. "My heart exults in the LORD... The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength" (1 Samuel 2:1, 4). Centuries later a young girl in Nazareth, carrying a King no palace asked for, will sing it back: "He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate" (Luke 1:52). The God of the empty woman is the God of the empty manger and the borrowed tomb. He chose what is low and despised, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are (1 Corinthians 1:28).

And then Hannah does the unthinkable. She gives the boy back. When he is weaned she carries him to Shiloh and leaves him there, with Eli, in the house of God. "For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD" (1 Samuel 1:27–28). The son she begged for, the son who answered twenty years of grief, she hands to a priest whose own house is rotting, and she walks home and sings. That is what an open hand looks like at the end. Not gritted endurance. A song. The greater David begins exactly where Samuel begins, in the place the strong overlook, given by a mother who would not hold him back, on his way to the deliverance of a people who did not yet know how empty they were.

God begins where you are emptied.

## Sons of Eli, Son of Hannah
*Two houses serving the same altar, and the God who will not be honored by men who despise Him*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 2:12–36 · **Supporting:** Malachi 2:7–8; Galatians 6:7; Hebrews 12:6; 1 Peter 4:17

The most dangerous men in Israel were not the Philistines outside the camp. They were the two priests inside the tabernacle, wearing the right clothes, handling the holy things, and despising every one of them.

**Contempt for God can wear a priest's robe.**
The writer names it without flinching. "Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:12). They served at the altar daily and did not know the one they served. They had access without reverence, proximity without fear. When the people came to sacrifice, the priests' servant would come with a three-pronged fork and take whatever it brought up, and if a man tried to give God the fat first, as the law required, the servant said give it now, "and if not, I will take it by force" (1 Samuel 2:16). "Thus the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt" (1 Samuel 2:17). They turned worship into extortion. They made the people loathe the offering of the LORD. And it was not their distance from the altar that did it. It was their nearness, abused. The prophet Malachi names the office they betrayed: "The lips of a priest should guard knowledge... For he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts. But you have turned aside from the way" (Malachi 2:7–8).

And the contempt was not only at the table. The writer adds a second charge, quietly, and it is worse. "They lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting" (1 Samuel 2:22). They used the house of God for their appetites, both kinds, and the worshipers saw it. A man came to bring God his best and watched the priest steal it and defile the doorway. How long before that man stopped coming? How long before he decided the God whose servants behaved like this was not worth the trip? That is the damage worthless leadership does. It does not only sin. It teaches the people that God can be despised, and they learn the lesson from the men who handle the holy things.

We assume the threat to the church is always outside the walls. The book of 1 Samuel opens by telling us the threat is at the altar, holding the fork.

**Eli grieved the sin and would not stop it.**
And here is the harder word, because it is not aimed at the obvious villains. It is aimed at the father who knew. Eli was not Hophni and Phinehas. Eli was grieved. He heard of all they did, and he said, "Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all the people" (1 Samuel 2:23–24). He spoke. He disapproved. He felt the right things. And it changed nothing, because feeling the right thing is not the same as doing the costly thing. He had the authority to remove them from the altar. He did not use it. So God sends a man with a verdict that lands on Eli, not only on his sons: "Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings... and honor your sons above me?" (1 Samuel 2:29).

That is the sentence I cannot get past. Honor your sons above me. Eli's sin was not contempt. It was a love that would not discipline, an affection that protected the very people destroying the worship of God. "The Lord disciplines the one he loves" (Hebrews 12:6), and Eli, loving his sons, would not. I know this temptation from the inside. I have softened a hard word because the person needed to hear it was someone I did not want to lose. I have called my cowardice patience. Eli is not a stranger to me. He is a mirror, and the man holding the mirror is a pastor.

And the warning Eli himself spoke should have stopped his own mouth. "If someone sins against a man, God will mediate for him, but if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?" (1 Samuel 2:25). He understood the theology perfectly. He could state the danger his sons were in with precision. And the writer adds the terrible note: "But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death." Knowing the right doctrine did not save Eli's house. Eli could diagnose the disease and would not perform the surgery. There are men who can preach against the very sin destroying their own homes, and the preaching costs them nothing because it never becomes action. I have been close enough to that man to recognize his handwriting.

**The child who grows in favor points past himself to the King who serves perfectly.**
The chapter keeps interrupting the house of Eli with a refrain about the house of Hannah. "Now the boy Samuel continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the LORD and also with man" (1 Samuel 2:26). Two houses serve the same altar. One despises the God it serves and is being torn down. One fears Him and is being raised up. The line between them is not talent or position. It is reverence. God is not mocked, and whatever a man sows, that he reaps (Galatians 6:7). Judgment, Peter says, begins at the household of God (1 Peter 4:17), and it began here, at the tabernacle, with the priests.

And the closing word is a promise of a better priest: "I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind" (1 Samuel 2:35). Samuel is the first answer. He is not the last. The line runs forward to the one priest who never treated His Father's offering with contempt, who honored God above every comfort, who did not extort the worshiper but became the sacrifice. The greater David is also the greater priest, the Son who did only what was in the Father's heart, all the way to a cross. Hophni and Phinehas grabbed the fat for themselves. He gave Himself away.

God is not mocked by His priests.

## A Word Becomes Rare, Then a Boy Hears
*When God falls silent on the failing, and speaks to a child who learns to repeat the hard word*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 3:1–4:1a · **Supporting:** Amos 8:11–12; Jeremiah 1:6–8; Acts 20:27; 2 Timothy 4:2

God went quiet on the priesthood of Israel. Then He skipped the priest entirely and woke a child in the dark.

**A rare word is a verdict before it is a circumstance.**
The chapter opens with a line that should frighten any church. "And the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision" (1 Samuel 3:1). Not because God had nothing to say. Because the people leading His worship had stopped listening, and a God who is not heard eventually stops being spoken of. Eli's eyes had grown dim so that he could not see (1 Samuel 3:2), and the writer means more than his eyes. The man who could not tell prayer from drunkenness in chapter one now cannot see in chapter three. The lamp of God had not yet gone out (1 Samuel 3:3), but it was guttering. Amos names this kind of silence as the worst famine God sends: "not a famine of bread... but of hearing the words of the LORD. They shall run to and fro... but they shall not find it" (Amos 8:11–12).

This is the part we get backward. We treat God's silence as His absence and our comfort as His blessing. Often it is the reverse. A church can be full and loud and busy and have no frequent vision, and not know it is starving, because it confused activity with hearing.

And notice where the famine had not reached. The lamp of God was in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was, and the boy Samuel was lying down there (1 Samuel 3:3). The structures were intact. The lamp still burned. The ark still sat in its place. The forms of the religion were all present and operating, and the word of God was rare in the middle of them. That is the most dangerous condition a people can be in, full equipment, empty heaven, because the equipment convinces them nothing is wrong. The lamp is still lit. The doors still open. And no one is hearing a thing.

**God bypasses the office and calls the child.**
Then, in the dark, a voice. "Samuel." And the boy runs to Eli, because where else would the word of God come from but the priest? Three times he runs to the wrong man. Three times Eli sends him back. And the writer slips in the reason Samuel could not place the voice: "Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him" (1 Samuel 3:7). The point is not that Samuel was slow. The point is that God's voice had become so unfamiliar in the house of God that no one recognized it, not the boy, and not, at first, the priest.

But Eli, blind as he is, gets one thing right, and it may be the best thing he ever does. He tells the boy what to say. "Speak, LORD, for your servant hears" (1 Samuel 3:9). The failing priest teaches the future prophet how to listen. And God comes and stands, and Samuel answers as he was taught, and what God gives him is not comfort. It is the sentence against the house of the very man who just taught him to listen. "I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew" (1 Samuel 3:13).

**The first task of a prophet is to speak the hard word without softening it.**
Now watch the boy's morning, because this is where the prophet is made. "Samuel lay until morning... And Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1 Samuel 3:15). Of course he was afraid. The first word God ever gave him was a word of judgment against the man who raised him. Every instinct in the child said soften it, blur it, find a kinder version. And Eli demands the whole thing: "Do not hide it from me" (1 Samuel 3:17). So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him (1 Samuel 3:18). Nothing. Not the part that would wound the old man across the room.

This is the call I feel the weight of every week, and the place I most often fail it. Jeremiah, called as a youth, protested that he did not know how to speak, that he was only a youth. And God answered, "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you" (Jeremiah 1:7–8). Paul could say at the end, "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:27), the whole, not the comfortable portion. "Preach the word... reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience" (2 Timothy 4:2). We have built a thousand pulpits on the half of the counsel that does not cost us anything. I have stood in one of them and called the editing wisdom.

And look at what Eli does with the word that condemns him, because it is the one moment of grace in his whole sad story. He does not rage. He does not deny it or send the boy away. "It is the LORD; let him do what seems good to him" (1 Samuel 3:18). The man who would not discipline his sons at least would not fight the verdict of God. There is a hard mercy in receiving the word that undoes you. It does not reverse the judgment, Eli's house still falls. But it shows that even under sentence, a man can bow. And the boy who delivered that sentence learned, in that exchange, that the word of God is not softened for the people we love most. It is spoken, received, and left in the hands of God.

And then the verse that tells you the famine is over. "And the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground... And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD" (1 Samuel 3:19–20). The word that was rare is now spoken from one end of the land to the other, through a boy who did not soften it. Samuel is the foreshadow of the Prophet to come, the greater David's greater forerunner, and finally of the Word Himself, who spoke the whole counsel and hid nothing, even the part that put Him on a cross.

Speak the word you were given.

## The Glory Has Departed
*A religion that wants God's power without God Himself, and the day He let it lose*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 4:1b–22 · **Supporting:** Jeremiah 7:4; Psalm 78:60–61; John 6:26; 2 Timothy 3:5

Israel lost a battle, so they sent for the ark. They did not send for repentance. They sent for the box.

**They wanted the power of God without the God of power.**
The Philistines struck first and killed about four thousand men on the field (1 Samuel 4:2). And the elders of Israel asked exactly the right question and reached exactly the wrong answer. "Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines?" (1 Samuel 4:3). That is the question of a people about to repent. But they do not finish it. They do not ask what they had done. They ask what they could deploy. "Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here... that it may save us" (1 Samuel 4:3). Not the LORD may save us. It may save us. The ark. The object. And who carried it into camp? "The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there" (1 Samuel 4:4), the worthless priests, the men who treated God's offering with contempt, marching God's throne into battle like a weapon.

The people shouted so the ground shook (1 Samuel 4:5). They had the noise of revival and the heart of none of it. This is the oldest religious error there is, and Jeremiah named it to a later generation standing in the same place: "Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD'" (Jeremiah 7:4). Say the holy thing three times and it becomes a charm. The form of religion stays. The fear of God is gone. "Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power" (2 Timothy 3:5).

And even the Philistines understood the theology better than Israel did. When they heard the shout and learned the ark had come into the camp, they were afraid, "for they said, 'A god has come into the camp.' And they said, 'Woe to us. Who can deliver us from the power of these mighty gods?'" (1 Samuel 4:7–8). The pagans took the presence of God more seriously than His own people did. Israel treated the ark as a charm. The Philistines treated it as terror. One of those is closer to reverence, and it was not the Israelites. A people can hold the holiest object in the world in their hands and mean less by it than the enemies trembling across the field.

**God let the charm lose.**
And God did the thing no one in the camp imagined possible. He let His own ark be captured. "And the ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died" (1 Samuel 4:11). The slaughter was worse with the ark than without it, thirty thousand foot soldiers fell (1 Samuel 4:10). God would rather lose a battle and surrender His ark to pagans than ratify a religion that used Him without wanting Him. The psalmist later sang of this exact day: "He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh... and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe" (Psalm 78:60–61). He delivered His own glory to the enemy. On purpose. Because His people had reduced Him to a thing they could carry.

I know this religion from the inside, because I have practiced it. I have wanted the results of God's presence, the full room, the moved emotion, the sense of momentum, without wanting the holiness that presence demands. I have shouted until the ground shook and not asked the question the elders refused to finish: what have we done. We want God to win our battles. We are far less sure we want God.

And the tell is always the same. The ark religion never repents. It manages. When the first defeat came, Israel did not search itself; it reached for a strategy. We do the identical thing. The numbers drop, the culture turns, the room thins out, and our instinct is to find the technique, the program, the relevant approach that will turn it around, anything but the question the elders would not finish. We will change our methods endlessly and our hearts never, because changing the method costs nothing and changing the heart costs everything. A church can lose thirty thousand and still not ask what it did. It will only ask what else it can deploy.

**You cannot carry Him as a charm, but in Christ He came to carry us.**
The news reaches Shiloh, and Eli, ninety-eight and blind, hears the worst of it not when they say the army fell, not when they say his sons are dead, but when they say the ark of God has been captured. At that word he falls backward and breaks his neck (1 Samuel 4:18). And his daughter-in-law, in labor and dying, names her son with the verdict over the whole nation: "She named the child Ichabod, saying, 'The glory has departed from Israel,' because the ark of God had been captured" (1 Samuel 4:21–22). Ichabod. No glory. Not because God was weak. Because His people had treated Him as a tool, and He would not be a tool.

There is a crowd in the Gospels that does the same thing. They followed Jesus across the sea, and He saw straight through them: "You are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves" (John 6:26). The ark religion never died. We still come for the loaves and leave when He speaks the cost. But hear the turn, because the cross is the whole answer to Shiloh. Israel tried to carry God into the place of death to save themselves, and the glory departed. The greater David walked into the place of death Himself, carried nothing, and was abandoned by the Father so that the glory would never depart from His people again. "The glory has departed" became, at an empty tomb, the glory has come and will not leave. He is not a charm we carry. He is a King who carried us.

You cannot carry God like a charm.

## God Needs No Defense
*The day the LORD defended His own honor among His enemies, and Israel did nothing*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 5:1–7:1 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 42:8; Psalm 115:4–8; Exodus 14:14; Romans 12:19

The ark of God spent seven months as a prisoner of war. It conquered three Philistine cities, toppled a god, and broke an army, and not one Israelite lifted a finger.

**God in enemy territory is still God.**
The Philistines did what any victor does with a captured god. They put the ark of Israel in the temple of their own god, Dagon, as a trophy. The defeated deity laid at the feet of the victorious one. That was the theology of the ancient world: the stronger god owns the weaker. "And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD" (1 Samuel 5:3). They set Dagon back up. They came again. "The head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon was left" (1 Samuel 5:4). The hands and the head, power and rule, severed and lying at the door. The idol bowed to the box it was supposed to own.

Then God moved on the people. "The hand of the LORD was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrified and afflicted them with tumors" (1 Samuel 5:6). They sent the ark to Gath. The plague went to Gath. They sent it to Ekron, and the men of Ekron cried out, "They have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us" (1 Samuel 5:10). City to city, the captured God conquered His captors. This is the psalm made flesh: "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see" (Psalm 115:4–5). Dagon had a mouth and could not cry out when his own hands were cut off. The God of Israel had no statue in that temple at all, and He emptied three cities.

And watch the Philistines try to manage Him, because it is almost comic and entirely human. They set Dagon back up the first morning, as though the problem were a tipped statue and not the living God in the room. They moved the ark from city to city, passing the affliction along like men passing a burning coal hand to hand, each city begging the next to take it. "Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill us and our people" (1 Samuel 5:11). They could not keep Him and could not kill Him and could not ignore Him. He was a prisoner who ruled His prison. Every strategy the strongest army in the region devised against the God of a defeated people failed, because there was never a contest. There was only the question of how long it would take them to admit it.

**Israel is absent from its own deliverance.**
Look hard at this chapter for the thing that is not there. Israel. No army marches. No prophet prays the ark home. No deliverer arises. For seven months God defends His own name in the heart of enemy country, and His people are nowhere in the story. "I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other, nor my praise to carved idols" (Isaiah 42:8). He did not need them. He never did.

We forget this constantly, and our forgetting always takes the same shape, the shape of a man rushing to protect a God who is not in danger. I have done it from the pulpit. I have argued and strategized and defended the honor of God as though it were a fragile thing in my hands, as though He would lose were I to fall silent. The Philistines could not protect Dagon. We cannot threaten God's honor with our weakness, and we cannot rescue it with our strength. "The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent" (Exodus 14:14). The ark in Dagon's temple is that verse with no Israelite even present to hear it.

This is the anxious labor of so much of our religious life, the frantic guarding of a reputation that was never in our keeping. We treat unbelief as a threat to be neutralized rather than a person to be loved. We treat every challenge to the faith as a fire to be stamped out before it spreads, as though the truth of God were a small flame that our argument keeps alive. It is not. He toppled Dagon with no defender in the building. He can survive the questions of a skeptic and the mockery of a culture without my panic. The man who actually believes God defends His own name argues differently, slower, kinder, unafraid, because he is not protecting something fragile. He is bearing witness to something unbreakable.

**The God who defends Himself is the King who refused to.**
Finally the Philistines, terrified, build a cart and send the ark home with a guilt offering of gold (1 Samuel 6:4), pagans paying tribute to a God they could not hold. They put it on a new cart pulled by two milk cows that had never been yoked, cows whose calves were shut up at home, and the cows went straight up the road to Israel, lowing as they went, not turning to the right or the left (1 Samuel 6:12). Against every instinct of nature, the captured God drove Himself home. The men of Beth-shemesh looked into the ark and learned the same lesson the Philistines learned, that holiness is not safe, and God is not casual, and the ark came to rest at Kiriath-jearim (1 Samuel 7:1).

Here is the turn that makes the whole story Christian. The God who would not be defended, who cut off Dagon's hands and emptied Ekron and drove His own cart home, this same God came in the flesh and let Himself be captured. The greater David stood before His enemies and did not call down the affliction He had every right to send. "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God" (Romans 12:19), and He, who could have leveled His captors as He leveled Dagon, gave no answer. The God who needs no defense chose to be undefended, so that the enemies He could have destroyed could be saved. Vengeance was His. He drank it instead.

God defends Himself among His enemies.

## If You Return, Return Fully
*Half-repentance is no repentance, and the only real defense Israel ever had*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 7:2–17 · **Supporting:** Joel 2:12–13; Hosea 6:1–3; James 4:8; Deuteronomy 6:5

Twenty years the ark sat at Kiriath-jearim, and Israel did the thing that feels like repentance and changes nothing. They mourned.

**Lamenting the loss is not the same as turning from the sin.**
"From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years, and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD" (1 Samuel 7:2). Twenty years of lamenting. Two decades of feeling badly about how far things had drifted, of missing the days of God's nearness, of grief over the consequences of sin. And it accomplished nothing, because longing for the blessing is not the same as forsaking the idol. They wept over the absence of God. They had not yet removed the gods they kept beside Him.

So Samuel cuts through twenty years of religious sadness with one demand. "If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines" (1 Samuel 7:3). If. With all your heart. Put away. He will not accept the lament without the surrender. He names the price: serve Him only. Not Him also. Only. This is the prophet Joel's word, "Return to me with all your heart... and rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:12–13). Torn clothes are easy. Torn hearts cost everything. We are forever offering God the garment and keeping the heart.

And here is the trap in twenty years of lamenting. Grief feels like repentance. It uses the same tears, the same ache, the same longing for things to be right again. A man can weep over what his sin has cost him for two decades and never once turn from the sin itself, because the weeping is about the consequence, not the rebellion. Israel mourned the absence of God. They did not yet hate the gods that caused it. That is the difference between remorse and repentance, and it is the difference between a person who is sorry he got caught and a person who is done. The first cries. The second changes. Twenty years of the first had moved Israel exactly nowhere.

**Returning means letting go of what you kept on the side.**
And Israel does the thing the twenty years of mourning never did. "So the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and they served the LORD only" (1 Samuel 7:4). They removed them. The household gods, the fertility shrines, the spiritual insurance policies kept in the back room in case the LORD did not come through, gone. This is the command at the center of Israel's faith finally obeyed: "You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might" (Deuteronomy 6:5). All. The word that exposes every half-return.

I know the foreign gods do not announce themselves as gods. That is what makes them hard to put away. Mine never looked like idolatry while I held them. They looked like security. They looked like being prepared. They looked like the reasonable backup plan a sensible pastor keeps in case ministry, or money, or reputation should fail him. We do not bow to Ashtaroth. We keep a small one on the side, just in case, and call our hedging wisdom. Hosea knew the shape of true return: "Come, let us return to the LORD... Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD" (Hosea 6:1–3). Press on. Not mourn from a distance. Press on.

**God Himself becomes their defense, the work the King would finish.**
Now watch the order, because it is the gospel of the chapter. They repent first. The deliverance comes second. Samuel gathers them at Mizpah, and while he is offering a sacrifice and crying out to the LORD for Israel, the Philistines draw up to attack (1 Samuel 7:9–10). The enemy comes precisely when the people are unarmed and on their knees. And Israel does not win this battle. "But the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were routed before Israel" (1 Samuel 7:10). The LORD thundered. Not the army. Not Samuel's strategy. The same God who needed no defense in Dagon's temple now defends a repentant people who could not defend themselves. "Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners" (James 4:8). They drew near by putting away the idols. He drew near with thunder.

And Samuel takes a stone and sets it up and names the whole story: "Till now the LORD has helped us," and he called its name Ebenezer (1 Samuel 7:12). Stone of help. Not stone of our courage. Not stone of our comeback. A monument to a battle the people watched God win after they finally let go of what they had kept on the side. The Philistines were subdued and did not again enter the territory of Israel all the days of Samuel (1 Samuel 7:13).

That stone points down the road to a hill where the real Ebenezer stands. Israel's repentance brought God's thunder. But the greater David did what no half-returning people could ever do, He returned to the Father with a whole heart no idol had ever divided, and when the thunder of judgment came, it fell on Him. We could not put away our gods. He put away our guilt. The stone of help is finally a cross, and the help it marks is not that God helped us win, but that He won it Himself and called us home.

Repentance is the only real defense.

## Give Us a King Like the Nations
*The day Israel asked God to stop being their King*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 8:1–22 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 17:14–20 · Judges 8:23 · 1 Samuel 12:17 · Hosea 13:11

Israel did not ask for a bad king. They asked for a king at all. And that was the sin.

**The request that sounded reasonable**
Read the demand slowly, because everything turns on a single word. "Samuel was old and had made his sons judges over Israel." They "did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice" (1 Samuel 8:1–3). So the elders come with a case that any of us would sign. "You are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5). Notice what they get right. The corruption is real. Samuel's sons are taking bribes; the leadership is failing; the succession is broken. They diagnosed the problem correctly. And then they reached for the wrong cure. This is how almost every idol enters a life. Not through a lie we can see, but through a true grievance and a wrong answer to it. We are not usually seduced by what is obviously evil. We are seduced by a real wound and a counterfeit healing. The elders were not wrong that something was broken. They were wrong about what would fix it. And there is a second thing buried in their request that we read right past. God had already anticipated this exact moment. Generations earlier, in the law of Moses, He had said, "When you come to the land that the LORD your God is giving you... and then say, 'I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,' you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose" (Deuteronomy 17:14–15). So a king was not forbidden. God had made room for one. The sin was not the office. The sin was the heart that demanded it, the phrase "like all the nations" that Israel echoed back word for word, the longing to be ordinary, the desire for a security they could see. The problem was never the institution. The problem was always the trust underneath it.

**The rejection underneath the request**
God's answer to Samuel strips the diplomacy away. "They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them" (1 Samuel 8:7). There it is. The whole arc of Israel had been a people with no king but Yahweh, the God who heard them in Egypt, split the sea, fed them in the wilderness, fought their battles when they had no army and no chariots. Gideon had already named the temptation and refused it: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you" (Judges 8:23). To ask for a king "like all the nations" was to ask to stop being the one nation that was not like the nations. It was to trade the invisible King who could not be managed for a visible king who could be paraded. And here is the part we keep missing about idolatry. The deepest sin is rarely the worship of something hideous. It is the relocation of trust from the God we cannot control to a thing we can see, touch, and put on a throne. Different object. Same human heart, choosing the manageable god over the living one. So God tells Samuel to do the most frightening thing in the chapter. "Obey their voice" (1 Samuel 8:9). Grant it. Some judgments arrive as a no. This one arrives as a yes. He gives them exactly what they asked for, and that is the verdict.

**The king who will take**
Then comes the warning, and it lands like a hammer falling six times. Samuel tells them "the ways of the king who shall reign over them." He will take your sons for his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of your grain, your flocks, your servants. "And you shall be his slaves" (1 Samuel 8:11–17). One verb runs the whole passage like a drumbeat, take, take, take, take, take. The God they were rejecting was the God who gave. Manna in the morning. Water from rock. A land they did not clear. The king they craved would do the one thing Yahweh never did. He would take. And the most sobering line is the last: "In that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day" (1 Samuel 8:18). The idol you demand becomes the master you serve. Long before God formally warns of this through Hosea, "I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath" (Hosea 13:11), the pattern is already set here. We did the choosing. We will do the crying. And we will not be able to say we were not told. Now turn the mirror, because we have been describing ancient Israel and letting ourselves off. We have wanted a savior we could see. We have wanted leaders, programs, marriages, careers, and political men to do for us what only God can do, and we have called that demand wisdom. I have stood in a pulpit and asked God for outcomes I could manage instead of the God I could not. We are the elders at Ramah. And the deepest mercy in this whole chapter is the one Israel could not yet see. God let them have their king, and then, centuries later, He sent the true one. Not a king who takes. A King who gives Himself. The greater David did not conscript sons for His chariots; He gave His own life for His enemies. He did not take a tenth; He emptied Himself entirely. "The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." Israel asked for a king like the nations and got Saul, who would take everything. God answered the demand under the demand by sending a King unlike any nation has ever seen, one who reigns by dying.

Be careful what you demand from God.

## The Tall Man Hiding in the Baggage
*God anoints the king the people wanted, and shows you the crack in him*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 9:1–10:27 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 10:6 · 1 Samuel 10:22 · 1 Samuel 16:7 · Proverbs 29:25

Israel wanted a king like the nations, and God gave them a man who looked the part exactly. That is the warning hiding in plain sight.

**The man who looked like the answer**
The text introduces Saul the way a casting director would. "There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish... a man of wealth. And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people" (1 Samuel 9:1–2). Read that twice. The first thing Scripture tells us about Saul is his height and his face. Not his faith. Not his fear of the Lord. His shoulders. This is the king the people asked for, described in the only terms a crowd that wanted to be "like the nations" could understand. He is the man you would pick. He is the man any of us would pick. And the whole book is about to teach us why the picking went wrong. The mechanism God will name explicitly to Samuel a few chapters later is already operating here in the description itself: "Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). We meet Saul through human eyes first, on purpose. The text lets us admire him exactly as Israel admired him, so that it can show us the difference between stature and a settled heart. And we do this every day. We size up a leader by his presence, a candidate by his bearing, a man by his shoulders. We trust the tall and the handsome and the confident because something in us believes that what looks strong is strong. Israel wanted to be like the nations, and the nations crowned the men who looked the part. So God gave them a man who looked the part more than any other man alive, and then spent the rest of the book showing them what the part is worth when the heart is not in it. The first thing we are told about Saul is the first thing we always notice about anyone. It is also the least reliable.

**The God who gives and confirms**
And yet, this is the part the cynical reading misses, God is genuinely generous to Saul. The whole encounter is laced with grace he did not earn. He goes looking for lost donkeys and stumbles into a kingdom. Samuel feeds him the choicest portion at the feast, set aside before he arrived. Samuel anoints him privately and says, "Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel?" (1 Samuel 10:1). Then God hands him gift after gift. Confirming signs along the road. Men who will meet him, bread that will be given to him, a band of prophets. And most stunning of all: "the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man" (1 Samuel 10:6). "God gave him another heart" (1 Samuel 10:9). Let that stand. The Spirit rushed on Saul. God gave him a new heart and confirming signs and a prophet to mentor him and a private anointing soaked in honor. Whatever later happens to Saul, it does not happen because God was stingy at the start. The beginning of Saul is grace upon grace. Which makes the ending more sobering, not less. A man can receive the Spirit's rush and the gift of another heart and the favor of God's prophet, and still come apart. The equipping was real. The equipping was not the same as the man.

**The crack at the coronation**
Then comes the coronation, and the camera catches something the crowd almost misses. Samuel gathers the tribes at Mizpah to present the king publicly, casting lots until the lot falls on Saul. "But when they sought him, he could not be found" (1 Samuel 10:21). The king of Israel is missing at his own crowning. "So they inquired again of the LORD, 'Is there a man still to come?' and the LORD said, 'Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage'" (1 Samuel 10:22). Picture it. The tallest man in Israel, head and shoulders above everyone, crouched down among the supply wagons. The man chosen precisely because he was impossible to miss, hiding. There is a kind of humility we are tempted to praise here, and I will not praise it, because the book will not. This is not the humility that fears God. This is the timidity that fears people. "The fear of man lays a snare" (Proverbs 29:25), and Saul is already in it. The same man who hides in the baggage today will, a few chapters from now, disobey God because "I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24). The crack is the same crack. He cares more about the crowd in front of him than the God above him, and at the coronation that crack looks almost like modesty. It is not. It is the fault line that will run the length of his reign. Now turn it on us, because we have all hidden in the baggage and called it humility. We have shrunk from what God plainly called us to and named our cowardice meekness. We have let the fear of people decide what the fear of God should have decided, and we have dressed it up as not wanting to seem proud. I have done this in my own ministry and called it discernment. The contrast the whole book is driving toward stands behind every line. There is another King who was anointed by the Spirit, who also stood head and shoulders above the people, not in stature, but in righteousness, and who did not hide. When the soldiers came for the greater David in the garden, He did not crouch among the baggage. He stepped forward: "Whom do you seek?" He went toward the cross the people demanded, not because He feared the crowd, but because He loved them. Saul was tall and hid. Christ was lowly and stepped into the open. One had stature. The other had a heart.

Stature is not the same as a heart.

## A Real Victory and a Sober Farewell
*The king finally fights, and the prophet says it changes nothing about the demand*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 11:1–12:25 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 11:6 · 1 Samuel 12:12 · 1 Samuel 12:23–24 · Joshua 24:15

Saul wins his first battle, and it is a genuine, Spirit-driven, life-saving victory. And then Samuel stands up and refuses to let the victory cover the sin underneath it.

**The victory that was real**
We should not be stingy with Saul here, because the text is not. Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and offers terms that are pure cruelty. "On this condition I will make a treaty with you, that I gouge out all your right eyes" (1 Samuel 11:2). The town sends for help, the news reaches Saul, and then something happens that is the best thing said about him in the whole book. "And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1 Samuel 11:6). The same Spirit that rushed on him at his anointing rushes on him now, and Saul acts. He rallies Israel, marches through the night, and routs the Ammonites "so that no two of them were left together" (1 Samuel 11:11). Jabesh is saved. The eyes are spared. And then the man who hid in the baggage does something genuinely worthy. When the people want to execute the men who had earlier doubted him, Saul refuses: "Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel" (1 Samuel 11:13). Give him this day. It was a real victory, won by a real anointing, and he gave the glory to the right place. The Spirit was on him; the rescue was God's; Saul, for one shining chapter, was the king Israel hoped for. We are not asked to pretend the good was not good. We are asked to see that the good was not enough.

**The farewell that named the sin**
Because then Samuel stands up. They go to Gilgal, renew the kingdom, and offer sacrifices, and into that celebration the old prophet steps to give his farewell address, and he will not let a battlefield victory erase a covenant betrayal. He recites the whole history of God's faithfulness, the deliverance from Egypt, judge after judge raised up in mercy. And then he names the thing they wanted everyone to forget. "When you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, 'No, but a king shall reign over us,' when the LORD your God was your king" (1 Samuel 12:12). There it is, set down in the record. The demand for a king was not a neutral administrative choice. It was the rejection of God's kingship, and one good battle does not undo it. This is the move we cannot afford to miss, because we run from it constantly. We treat a later success as proof that an earlier sin was actually fine. The marriage that survives the affair. The ministry that grows after the compromise. The decision made in unbelief that happened to turn out well. And we conclude: see, it worked, so it must have been right. Samuel will not let Israel reason that way. The kingdom is established; the victory is real; and the demand was still rebellion. So he asks God to send thunder and rain in the dry wheat harvest, an impossibility, and God does it, and "all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel" (1 Samuel 12:18). The lesson lands in their bones. "We have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king" (1 Samuel 12:19). Outcome does not sanctify rebellion. The win was real. The sin was also real. Both, at once.

**The demand that now binds them all**
And here is where Samuel does his most pastoral and most terrifying work. He does not leave them in despair. "Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil. Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart" (1 Samuel 12:20). The door is open. The covenant still stands. But the terms are now plain, and they fall on everyone, king and people alike, the same demand laid on both. "If you still do wickedly, you shall be swept away, both you and your king" (1 Samuel 12:25). There is no special exemption for the man with the crown. The king they wanted in order to feel safe now stands under the same word they do: fear the Lord, or be swept away together. The choice is the old Joshua choice given new urgency, "choose this day whom you will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15). And turn this on us before we close, because we have all wanted the king and the safety more than we wanted the Lord. We have wanted a leader, a system, a strong man to stand between us and Nahash so we would not have to trust God in the dark. And when it works for a season, we call our unbelief prudence. We are Israel at Gilgal, relieved and indicted in the same breath. But hear the mercy Samuel could not yet fully see. The last word from this old shepherd is not condemnation but intercession: "Far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you" (1 Samuel 12:23). A faithful man stands between a guilty people and judgment, refusing to stop praying for them. That is a shadow of the greater David, the true and faithful King who would not be swept away with His people but stood in their place, the King who fears the Lord perfectly on our behalf, and who ever lives to make intercession for us. Saul could win a battle. Only Christ could keep the covenant we broke.

Fear the Lord, king and people both.

## The King Who Could Not Wait
*Seven days, an army on the hill, and a throne thrown away*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 13:1–14:52 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 13:13–14 · 1 Samuel 14:6 · 1 Samuel 15:22 · Isaiah 7:9

Saul lost a dynasty not because he refused to worship, but because he worshiped at the wrong moment to avoid obeying. That is the danger we never see coming.

**The pressure that felt like an excuse**
The scene is built to make us sympathize with Saul, which is exactly the point. The Philistines muster against Israel with "thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore" (1 Samuel 13:5). Saul's men are watching this army gather, and they are coming apart. "The people were hard pressed... the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns" (1 Samuel 13:6). Saul's own troops are slipping away, deserting daily, and he is waiting at Gilgal for Samuel, who said he would come in seven days to offer the sacrifices. The seventh day arrives. Samuel does not. The army is melting. And Saul does the thing that any pressured leader would feel justified in doing. "So Saul said, 'Bring the burnt offering here to me'... And he offered the burnt offering" (1 Samuel 13:9). He took the priestly role that was never his to take. And here is what we have to feel before we judge it: it looked responsible. It looked like leadership. The men were scattering, the enemy was massing, the prophet was late, and somebody had to do something. Saul was not throwing a party. He was offering a sacrifice. He was being, by every outward measure, religious in a crisis. That is what makes this passage so dangerous to read comfortably. The sin does not look like sin. It looks like piety under pressure. And we should be honest about the math Saul was running, because we run it too. He was watching a real army. His men were really leaving. The prophet really was late. Every variable he could count was screaming at him to act, and the only thing telling him to wait was a word from God spoken seven days ago, with nothing visible to back it up. Saul trusted what he could see over what God had said. That is the whole of it. The chariots were in front of him; the command was behind him; and when the seen and the spoken came into conflict, he sided with his eyes. We call that being realistic. Scripture calls it foolish.

**The disobedience dressed as worship**
Samuel arrives the moment the offering is finished, and his verdict is immediate and total. "You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God, with which he commanded you... the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart" (1 Samuel 13:13–14). The whole dynasty, gone, over a sacrifice. And notice precisely what the sin was, because we will misread it otherwise. The sin was not irreverence. Saul was being reverent. The sin was that he used an act of worship as a substitute for an act of obedience. He could not wait, so he took control, and then he sanctified his impatience by calling it a burnt offering. When Samuel confronts him, listen to the self-justification: "I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come... so I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering" (1 Samuel 13:11–12). "I forced myself." He frames his disobedience as something he reluctantly had to do, even something costly. This is the exact lesson God will state outright two chapters later: "to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). Saul keeps offering God sacrifices instead of obedience, and God keeps refusing the trade. Because worship was never meant to be the thing you do instead of obeying. It was meant to be the thing you do because you trust the One you obey. Saul reached for the religious act to manage his anxiety, and in doing so revealed that he trusted the act more than the God it was supposed to honor. Religion without obedience is just anxiety in liturgical clothing.

**The son who trusted against the odds**
And the chapter sets a foil right next to him, his own son. While Saul counts his shrinking troops, Jonathan walks toward a Philistine garrison with one armor-bearer and a sentence that is everything Saul is not. "Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few" (1 Samuel 14:6). There is the heart Saul lacked. Jonathan does not know the outcome, "it may be", but he knows the God, and he acts on the God and not on the odds. "Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few." That is the faith Isaiah would later compress into a single line: "If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all" (Isaiah 7:9). The father, with the bigger title, counted heads and panicked. The son, with two men, trusted and God shattered an army. Now turn this on us, because we are Saul far more often than we are Jonathan. We reach for the religious thing when the obedient thing is too costly. We pray instead of forgiving the person we are commanded to forgive. We attend instead of repenting. We serve instead of submitting. We hand God our sacrifices so we can keep back our wills. I have done this from a pulpit, offered God impressive worship while withholding plain obedience, and called the worship enough. But there is a King who waited when Saul could not. In the wilderness, hungry and pressed, the greater David was offered every shortcut, and He refused each one. In the garden, with an army coming and the cup before Him, He did not seize control. He said, "Not my will, but yours, be done." He is the King after God's own heart that Samuel pointed toward, the one who obeyed perfectly under a pressure that would have shattered any of us, and obeyed all the way to a cross.

Obedience cannot be replaced by religion.

## To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice
*The day partial obedience was finally called what it is*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 15:1–35 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 15:22–23 · 1 Samuel 15:24 · Exodus 17:14 · 1 Samuel 16:7

Saul did most of what God commanded. And "most" is the word that cost him the kingdom.

**The command and the careful exception**
The command is severe, and we should not soften it, because the whole sermon depends on God meaning exactly what He said. Through Samuel, God tells Saul to devote Amalek to destruction, a long-standing judgment on a nation that had ambushed Israel's weak and weary in the wilderness, a judgment God Himself had pronounced generations earlier: "I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven" (Exodus 17:14). This is not Saul's whim; it is God's settled justice finally falling. "Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have" (1 Samuel 15:3). And Saul goes, and Saul fights, and Saul wins, almost completely. "But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fattened calves and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction" (1 Samuel 15:9). Look at the precision of the disobedience. He destroyed the worthless and kept the valuable. He obeyed God in everything that cost him nothing and disobeyed God in everything that was worth keeping. This is not a man who ignored the command. This is a man who edited it. He kept the parts that were convenient and discarded the parts that were costly, and he did it with care. Partial obedience is not a smaller version of obedience. It is obedience with the self still firmly on the throne, choosing which of God's words it will honor. And notice the genius of how Saul sinned. He did not refuse God outright. An outright refusal he could not have lived with; it would have been too obviously rebellion. So instead he obeyed enough to feel obedient. He kept the form of the command and gutted its substance. He could stand before Samuel and say, with a clear conscience, that he had done what God asked, because he had done most of it, the visible most, the destruction of everything worthless. The kept sheep were tucked behind a technicality. This is how respectable people disobey God. Not with a clenched fist, but with a careful edit, leaving in just enough obedience to silence the conscience and keeping back the one thing the self refused to surrender.

**The worship that was rebellion**
And then comes the confrontation, and Saul's first words are the words of a man who genuinely believes he succeeded. "Blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD" (1 Samuel 15:13). He thinks he obeyed. That is the most frightening part of the whole chapter. He is not lying to Samuel so much as he has lied to himself. Then Samuel hears it, "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears, and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?" (1 Samuel 15:14). Caught, Saul does two things we all do. First he blames the people: "The people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen" (1 Samuel 15:15). Then he spiritualizes it: they kept the animals "to sacrifice to the LORD your God." He dressed his disobedience as worship. He kept what God said to destroy and called it an offering. And Samuel answers with the sentence that organizes this whole stretch of Scripture: "Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry" (1 Samuel 15:22–23). There is the verdict that strips off the costume. God names Saul's careful, religious, well-intentioned partial obedience by its real name: rebellion. Idolatry. Witchcraft. Not a lesser obedience, a different thing entirely, the same in kind as the darkest sins, because at the root of all of them is a self that will not yield. We keep thinking the issue is the size of the disobedience. God says the issue is the existence of it. A throne with God on it has no exceptions. And when Saul finally confesses, even the confession exposes him: "I have sinned... because I feared the people and obeyed their voice" (1 Samuel 15:24). The same fear of man that hid him in the baggage now spares Agag. He feared the people more than he feared God, and that fear chose which of God's words he would keep.

**The exceptions we keep for ourselves**
Now turn it on us, because we are all keepers of exceptions. We give God the worthless and spare the best. We obey Him everywhere it costs nothing and edit Him everywhere it costs something. We surrender the sins we did not want anyway and quietly keep the one we do. And like Saul, we have learned to spiritualize the keeping, to call our compromise wisdom, our cowardice peacemaking, our held-back idol a thing we are "still praying about." We blame the people. We frame our disobedience as worship. I have stood in a pulpit and preached surrender while keeping back an Agag of my own, and called the preaching obedience. The bleating gives us away every time. But hear where this points, because the chapter ends in grief, "Samuel grieved over Saul" (1 Samuel 15:35), and that grief is the door. The very next chapter sends Samuel to anoint a new king, and the standard is announced: "The LORD sees not as man sees... the LORD looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). God was not looking for a king with a better record. He was looking for a King with a yielded heart, and He found Him, ultimately, not in Bethlehem's shepherd but in the greater David who came from him. Where Saul kept back the best for himself, Christ kept back nothing. Where Saul spared what God said to give up, Christ gave up His own life and spared us. Where Saul obeyed in part, the true King "became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross." He is the obedience we never offered, given to us as a gift.

Partial obedience is still rebellion.

## The Lord Looks at the Heart
*God walks past everyone you would have chosen*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 16:1–23 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 16:7 · 1 Samuel 16:11–13 · 1 Corinthians 1:27 · Psalm 78:70–72

God sent His prophet to a house full of impressive men and chose the one nobody bothered to invite to dinner.

**The prophet still grieving the old king**
The chapter opens on a tired, grieving man. "The LORD said to Samuel, 'How long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel?'" (1 Samuel 16:1). Samuel is still mourning the king who looked the part and failed it, and God moves him forward, fill your horn, go to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, for "I have provided for myself a king among his sons." And here the whole drama is set, because Samuel is a man who has just been burned by appearances. He anointed a tall, handsome king once. He watched that king come apart over impatience and partial obedience and the fear of people. You would think the old prophet had learned. He had not. None of us has. When he arrives and Jesse's sons are presented, Samuel takes one look at the firstborn and his heart says yes. "When they came, he looked on Eliab and thought, 'Surely the LORD's anointed is before him'" (1 Samuel 16:6). Eliab is the obvious choice. Tall, no doubt. Impressive, surely. The eldest, the natural heir, the one any of us would have crowned on sight. Samuel is about to do the exact thing that went wrong with Saul, all over again, because the human eye does not learn. It keeps reaching for height and presence and the firstborn's face. And we should feel how reasonable Samuel's instinct was, because it is ours. Eliab was not a foolish guess. He was the obvious, defensible, sensible choice, the eldest, the impressive one, the man you would put forward in any room. If you were assembling a leader by every metric a search committee uses, you would land on Eliab and feel good about it. That is exactly the danger. The wrong choice here was not careless. It was careful. It was the trained eye of a seasoned prophet doing precisely what experience had taught him to do, and it was wrong, because experience had trained him to read the surface, and God reads something the surface never shows.

**The sentence that reorders everything**
And God stops him with the line that is the spine of the entire book. "Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). "The height of his stature", the very phrase used of Saul. God is correcting the old mistake by name. So Jesse parades seven sons past the prophet, and one by one God says no. Abinadab, no. Shammah, no. Seven impressive men, and the Lord has chosen none of them. "And Samuel said to Jesse, 'The LORD has not chosen these'" (1 Samuel 16:10). Then comes one of the quietest, most exposing lines in Scripture. Samuel asks if there are any more, and Jesse says, almost as an afterthought, "There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep" (1 Samuel 16:11). Out with the animals. Not invited to the sacrifice. Not considered worth presenting. His own father did not think to call him in. And God had chosen him before Samuel ever left home. "Arise, anoint him, for this is he" (1 Samuel 16:12). This is the mechanism that runs through the whole Bible: "God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong" (1 Corinthians 1:27). The shepherd boy who was an afterthought to his own family was God's settled choice, "He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds" (Psalm 78:70). God does not see what we see. He never has.

**The mirror we cannot trust**
Now turn this on yourself, because we are all in this house, and we are all looking at the wrong things. We measure people the way Samuel measured Eliab, height, presence, polish, the firstborn confidence, and we measure ourselves the same way, in the mirror, by the outward appearance. We build whole lives on what man sees: the platform, the resume, the face we present, the impression we manage. And underneath the impressive exterior God is looking at the one thing we work hardest to keep hidden, the heart, the actual seat of our loves and our trust and our rebellion, the room we never let anyone into. The terror and the mercy of 1 Samuel 16:7 are the same fact: God sees the part of you that your mirror cannot. I have spent years tending the outward man, the sermon, the title, the reputation, and God has been reading the heart the whole time, the one no congregation ever saw. That should frighten every one of us. And then it should free us, because of where this anointing points. The shepherd boy of Bethlehem, overlooked by his family and chosen by God, was a shadow of a greater Shepherd from the same town a thousand years later. The true and greater David came to a stable no one thought to look in, born to a people no one esteemed, and "he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him" (Isaiah 53:2). The world looked at the outward appearance and saw nothing worth choosing. God looked at the heart, the only heart that was ever wholly His, and crowned Him King over heaven and earth. The same God who looks past your mirror and sees the worst of you has set His love on you anyway, in the One whose heart was perfect in your place. He does not choose you because you are impressive. He never did. He chooses, and then He makes you new.

God sees what your mirror cannot.

## The Battle Belongs to the Lord
*A shepherd boy, a giant, and the name no army dared to use*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 17:1–58 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 20:1–4; Psalm 20:7; 2 Corinthians 10:4; Hebrews 11:32–34

An army can have armor, training, a king a head taller than every man in it, and still be undone by a single voice. Israel had all of that. For forty days they had none of it where it mattered.

**The fear that armor could not cover**
The scene is set with the care of a man who wants you to feel the standoff before you feel anything else. "And the Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with a valley between them" (1 Samuel 17:3). Into that valley walks a man whose every measurement the text insists on giving you, six cubits and a span, bronze on his head, bronze on his legs, a spear like a weaver's beam. And twice a day for nearly six weeks he says the same thing, and twice a day the response is the same. "When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid" (1 Samuel 17:11).

Notice who is missing from the fear. Not the cowards. The trained. The anointed king stands in his tent. The covenant army stands behind its shields. The God who had drowned Pharaoh's chariots and flattened Jericho's walls is not in their calculation at all. They are doing the math the world always does, his height against ours, his reach against ours, his iron against our nerve. And by that math they are right to be afraid.

That is the thing about fear. It is rarely irrational. Goliath is real. The arithmetic is honest. What fear cannot do is count the One it has left off the page.

**The boy who counted differently**
Then comes a shepherd, sent by his father to bring bread and cheese to his brothers, and he hears the giant, and he is not afraid. Not because he is braver. Because he is doing different math. While everyone else asks what Goliath is, David asks one question nobody else has thought to ask: "For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" (1 Samuel 17:26).

The living God. That is the term that has gone missing from an entire army's vocabulary for forty days. David is not measuring Goliath against Israel. He is measuring Goliath against Yahweh, and by that measure the giant shrinks to what he actually is, one uncircumcised man with a loud mouth and no covenant. This is the old word Moses gave a frightened army before they ever crossed the Jordan: "Do not fear or panic or be in dread of them, for the Lord your God is he who goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory" (Deuteronomy 20:3–4).

Watch what David refuses. He refuses Saul's armor, refuses to fight the Lord's battle by the world's measurements. And then he says the line the whole chapter has been building toward, and it is the most theologically loaded sentence a teenager has ever spoken on a battlefield: "You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. This day the Lord will deliver you into my hand... that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel" (1 Samuel 17:45–46).

Sword, spear, javelin, three pieces of iron, named in a row, the sum total of what Goliath trusts. Against all three, one name. And then the verdict that the whole valley needed to hear and only the boy would say: "For the battle is the Lord's" (1 Samuel 17:47).

**The fight you were never strong enough to win**
We read this and we do the very thing the chapter forbids. We make David the hero and ourselves the David, find your inner shepherd, name your giant, run at it. And we lie to ourselves the whole time, because we know what is in our tent. I have stood in front of my own Goliaths and reached for Saul's armor every time. I have trusted the chariot. I have done the world's math on my own marriage, my own fear, my own sin, and come back from the valley dismayed, and called it realism. Psalm 20:7 names exactly what we did: "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the Lord our God." Some of us. Not all of us. Not always us.

Here is what the chapter is doing, and it is not handing you a technique. It is handing you a king. Israel could not fight this battle. The army was right to be afraid by its own strength, it had none that mattered. So God sent a representative, one anointed man who would go down into the valley alone and fight the enemy the whole nation could not face, and win a victory the whole nation would share. The people did nothing. The champion did everything. And when he had won, the victory was counted to them.

That is not a story about your courage. That is the gospel in a valley. Centuries later another Son of David went down into a worse valley, alone, against an enemy no army could touch, and he did not fight with sword or spear but with a cross, and to every eye it looked like the giant had won. It looked like defeat. It was the deathblow. "For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). The greater David went into the ground and came out the other side with death's head in his hand, so that all the earth would know there is a God in Israel.

You are not the shepherd in this story. You are the trembling army on the hillside, watching a champion fight the battle you could never win.

The fight belongs to your God.

## When a Song Turns a Heart to Murder
*How a tune in the street becomes a spear against the wall*

**Text:** 1 Samuel 18:1–30 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 14:30; James 3:16; Genesis 4:5–8; 1 Samuel 16:14

A king lost his kingdom not in a battle but in a chorus. The giant could not bring Saul down. A women's song did.

**The line that landed wrong**
Israel comes home from the valley singing, and the song is a good song, a true song. "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7). It is celebration, not insult. The women are dancing, the tambourines are out, the nation is glad. And one man in the parade hears the same words everyone else hears and something inside him curdles. "And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, 'They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?'" (1 Samuel 18:8).

The text tells you the exact moment the rot begins. "And Saul eyed David from that day on" (1 Samuel 18:9). One song. One comparison. From that day on he could not look at David without measuring himself against him and coming up short.

Nothing changed in David. He was still the same loyal servant who had killed the giant for Saul's army. What changed was the king's eye. Jealousy is not information about the other person. It is a sickness in the one who carries it, and it always tells the same lie, that another man's gift is a theft from you, that his thousands are subtracted from yours. Proverbs names it with surgical plainness: "A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot" (Proverbs 14:30). Saul's bones began to rot to the sound of music in the street.

**From the eye to the spear**
Watch how fast envy travels once it is fed. The very next day "a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house while David was playing the lyre... And Saul had his spear in his hand. And Saul hurled the spear, for he thought, 'I will pin David to the wall'" (1 Samuel 18:10–11). The man playing music to soothe the king is now a target for the king's spear. And when the spear misses, Saul does not stop, he gets careful. He sends David away as a commander, hoping the Philistines will do what the spear could not. He offers him a daughter as a snare. He sets a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping David will die collecting it.

This is what James warned us about, and he warned us because he had seen it: "For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice" (James 3:16). Envy never stays a feeling. It is the architect of schemes. It dresses murder up as a wedding and calls a death trap a promotion. And the cruelest detail is that every plan fails the same way: "But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them" (1 Samuel 18:16). The more Saul tries to destroy him, the more the Lord is with him, and the more the people love him, which means the more the king has to hate.

We have a record of this exact mechanism from the fourth chapter of the Bible. Cain brings his offering and it is not accepted, and instead of grief that turns to repentance, he grows hot with envy at a brother whose offering was. "So Cain was very angry, and his face fell." God comes to him personally, warns him at the door, "sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it." And Cain hears the warning and walks his brother into a field anyway (Genesis 4:5–8). Same eye. Same falling face. Same crouching thing at the door. The first murder in human history was a jealous brother who would not rule the thing God told him to rule.

**The house divided against itself**
While the king's heart hardens, his own son's heart goes the other way. "The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1 Samuel 18:1). The heir to the throne strips off his robe and his armor and gives them to the man who will take his crown. Saul looks at David and sees a thief. Jonathan looks at the same man and sees a soul to bind himself to. One song, two hearts, and the house of Saul splits down the middle, father against son, throne against love.

And I have to be honest about which heart is more native to me. It is not Jonathan's. I have heard another man praised and felt the cold thing move in my chest. I have called another man's thousands a threat to my own. I have eyed a brother from that day on and told myself it was discernment. The pulpit does not protect you from this. It feeds it. Every comparison is a spear I am tempted to throw, and I have thrown more than I will admit.

Here is the mercy buried in the misery of this chapter. There was a King who heard the crowd cry up another and felt no spear rise in his hand, because the greater David did not grasp at a throne. He gave one up.
